relationship: An aspect-blind reader encodes the sentence without the aspect, as a dual encoder scores a document without the query; letting the aspect query the words is the cross-encoder's move, and Proposition 1 is the price of not making it.

Its Nadaraya–Watson estimator is what one aspect-query attention layer computes: a kernel-weighted average of the words' values whose kernel factors into a content part and a distance-to-the-aspect part, the position kernel of Definition 2.
Proposition 2's tone rule is multinomial naive Bayes on the counts of positive, neutral, and negative sentences with known parameters, which is why its accuracy is the corpus's Bayes ceiling.
On equispaced keys around a circle, attention is diagonalized by the Fourier basis, and its exact risk is computed by Parseval's identity from the Bessel gains.
Attention's output is the conditional mean of a kernel density estimate whose components sit on the keys, so its weights are the mixture's posterior responsibilities.
That page prices attention's quadratic cost in long contexts; this page factors the kernel with random features to make it linear, and measures what the factorization loses.
ColBERT's MaxSim keeps each query token's best-matching document token, the zero-temperature limit of the attention lookup analyzed here.
Softmax attention is its Nadaraya–Watson estimator with a Gaussian kernel and key-norm design weights; on the circle its bias–variance trade-off and AMISE rate become an exact closed form.
A Gaussian-process posterior mean is also a linear smoother of the responses, but it inverts the kernel matrix where Nadaraya–Watson and attention only normalize each row.
Graph attention aggregates a node's neighbors with softmax weights, which is this page's kernel smoother restricted to a neighborhood of the graph.

Prefix log-probabilities form a monotone non-increasing sequence, which is all that Theorems 1 and 3 use, and Proposition 3's normalized scores form a monotone bounded sequence whose limit is never attained (its Theorem 1).

Every edge weight on this page is a surprisal, −log p, its Definition 1's information content; the greedy regularizer and uniform information density are statements about how surprisal is spread along a string.
Decoding the mode is mode-seeking taken to its limit, the behavior that topic's section on forward and reverse KL contrasts with mode-covering fits.

Beam search is a deterministic cousin of particle resampling: it keeps the k heaviest partial strings where a particle filter resamples by weight (its resampling schemes of §4), and it collapses onto a few lineages the same way.

Its Corollary 1, Bonferroni's inequality, is the lower half of Proposition 1: the share of facts that survive both the entity and the relation stage is at least the sum of the two stage recalls minus one.
Its Theorem 4, Rao–Blackwell, says conditioning on more information never increases risk; Theorem 2(a) is the same comparison run backward, from a richer input to a coarser function of it.

Its Theorem 3, Efron–Bickel–Freedman consistency, underlies Proposition 4's cluster bootstrap of the Shapley shares, which resamples the 22 companies and recomputes every coalition's F1 from pooled counts.
Its Theorem 2, the recall pinch, says an oracle reranker can recover only what the pool holds: a one-stage ceiling analysis, which Theorem 1 here generalizes to every order of every stage.

Its Theorem 4, the data processing inequality, says processing cannot create information; Theorem 2(a) here is its decision-theoretic counterpart: a successor that receives the argmax instead of the posterior cannot have lower Bayes risk.
Its Theorem 7.1, the Bayes-optimal decision rule, is the rule that Theorem 2(a) compares across the two inputs a pipeline stage can hand on, the posterior and its argmax.

Its Theorem 4, the Banach contraction mapping theorem, gives Theorem 3's unique stationary distribution once the Google matrix contracts the simplex in ℓ1, and its Example 14, the Bellman operator, is the same discounted form.

Its Definitions 5 and 6 are the generalized likelihood ratio and its rejection rule, and its Theorem 4 is Wilks' theorem for a scalar parameter; its Remark 13 states the vector case without proof, and Theorem 2 here proves the 2×2 case directly.
Its Definition 12 states Pearson's goodness-of-fit statistic and its χ² limit; Proposition 1 and Theorem 2 here prove that limit for the independence test of a 2×2 table.

Its Theorems 15–17 give the hypergeometric distribution's moments and binomial limit, and its Example 6 computes Fisher's exact test as a hypergeometric tail; Lemma 1 here is why that tail is the exact null distribution.
Its Theorem 9, continuous mapping, and Theorem 10, Slutsky's theorem, carry Theorem 2's proof from the central limit theorem to the χ² limits of X² and G².
Its Theorem 1 (Bonferroni) and Theorem 5 (Benjamini–Hochberg) are the corrections Proposition 5 applies to the finance bigrams, once over the observed pairs and once over all candidate pairs.

Its Definition 4 and Theorem 1 weight a term inside one collection by its document frequency there; keyness instead tests a word's rate in one corpus against another, a different question the remark after Proposition 6 separates.
Its Definition 1, precision at a cutoff, is how the finance case study scores every ranking of bigrams and keywords against the generator's answer key.

Its Theorem 1 gives the stationary distribution of a walk on an undirected graph, proportional to degree, and its Theorem 3 the convergence of an ergodic walk; Proposition 7 here uses both, and Theorem 3 here proves the teleporting walk its PageRank remark describes.

Its Definition 5 is mutual information and its Proposition 6 says it vanishes exactly under independence; Theorem 1 here shows G² is 2N times the empirical mutual information of a bigram's two indicators.
The multivariate chain rule (its Theorem 2) is the encoder's hand-written backward pass through attention, the MLP, and LayerNorm, checked against central differences.
Bayes' theorem (its Theorem 4) applied to the corruption channel is the closed form of the masked-LM optimum at a mask, a kept token, or a random one.
The MLE's consistency (its Theorem 3) is the benchmark that pseudo-likelihood trades away, giving up efficiency for conditionals that need no normalizing constant.
A Gibbs sampler (its Theorem 2) needs conditionals that come from one joint; the four-cycle test shows a masked LM's do not, so Gibbs-style generation from BERT samples no stated distribution.
A dual encoder takes a pretrained encoder as given and trains it contrastively; this topic is where that encoder's token vectors come from and what geometry they have.
It names the anisotropic cone of contextual embeddings as the first way real data break von Mises–Fisher isotropy; the geometry section here measures the cone layer by layer.
SPLADE's term weights are log(1 + ReLU) of masked-LM logits, the very head this topic trains and whose optimum it computes.

Denoising autoencoders (its Theorem 3.2), masked autoencoding, and the linear probe (its Definition 9.1): BERT is the masked autoencoder for text, and this topic computes its optimum and probes its vectors.
The cross-entropy decomposition (its Proposition 1) and Gibbs' inequality (its Proposition 2) are the whole proof that the masked-LM risk is minimized by the true posterior.
PCA as optimal projection (its Theorem 2): maximum explainable variance is the share of a word's occurrence cloud that one principal direction carries, the best a static vector can do.
The series of log(1 + x) shows that PMI removes the background near independence and that a mixture's PMI departs from low rank only at second order.
Under independence a pair's co-occurrence count is Poisson, and that model shows why positive PMI on rare pairs is mostly a false positive.
Positive PMI tests every word pair at once against independence; its false positives concentrate on rare pairs, a multiple-testing problem that a likelihood-ratio test addresses.
Both pages use pointwise mutual information: there it scores what a retrieved document adds to an answer, here it is a word-association matrix estimated from counts and factorized.
Word vectors are compared by the cosine defined there; PMI reweights a word's co-occurrence row as IDF reweights a document's term vector, against a background rate.
Latent semantic analysis is the truncated SVD of a term-document matrix; document-level co-occurrence here is that matrix's Gram matrix, reweighted by PMI.
Truncated SVD gives the word vectors, and Eckart–Young says the word-by-context product is the best rank-d approximation of the PMI matrix; this page proves what word-by-word products approximate.
A symmetric window makes the PMI matrix symmetric, and its eigendecomposition shows why half-power word vectors misread its negative eigenvalues and why adding context vectors removes them.
The average PMI of a word over its own contexts is the KL divergence from the corpus's context distribution, and its frequency-weighted sum is the mutual information of words and contexts.
The exponentiated PMI matrix is the density ratio of the joint word–context distribution to the product of its marginals; mixtures make this ratio, not its logarithm, low rank.
Word vectors are an uncentered truncated SVD of a sparse PMI matrix, not PCA: centering would destroy sparsity, and the eigenvalue weight replaces PCA's variance scaling.
Its Theorem 2, the multivariate chain rule, gives the factored gradient of Theorem 1(a) and the Jacobian J whose Gram matrix is Proposition 5's kernel.

Its Theorem 5, the correspondence between a penalty and a prior, makes L2-SP a Gaussian prior centered at the pretrained weights, and its Remark 4, ridge along the singular vectors, is Proposition 3's shrinkage of the fine-tuning displacement.
Its Theorem 2 bounds the rank of the score matrix a dual encoder can produce; this page bounds the rank of a weight update instead, a different object with the same low-rank arithmetic.

Its Theorem 2, the Eckart–Young–Mirsky theorem, says the truncated SVD is the best rank-r approximation of a matrix; Proposition 2 uses it to ask how much of full fine-tuning's update a rank-r update could have captured.
Its Definition 9.1 is the linear probe, a classifier on frozen features, which is the first of this page's three adaptations and the head that LP-FT starts from.

Its Theorem 1, the Marchenko–Pastur limit, gives the spectrum a Gaussian matrix would have, the yardstick against which full fine-tuning's update is shown to be low-rank, and its lazy-training section is the regime of Proposition 5's kernel.

Elastic weight consolidation replaces L2-SP's identity by the Fisher information, the Riemannian metric of that topic, so that a penalty toward the old weights is weighted by how much each direction mattered.
Taylor's theorem with the Lagrange remainder sandwiches the Poisson cell loss between two quadratics, which is how GloVe's least squares approximates it.
GloVe's weighted least squares on log counts is one Fisher-scoring step of a Poisson regression with log link at the saturated fit, with the Fisher weight tempered.
Alternating least squares solves GloVe one block at a time, each word's vector and bias by the normal equations of a weighted ridge regression.
A ridge penalty on word and context vectors with free biases makes every stationary point balanced and centered: the penalty chooses the geometry the loss leaves free.
The Poisson log-partition supplies the Bregman divergence whose quadratic is GloVe's loss, with curvature equal to the count.
Analogy answers and benchmark scores here are cosine comparisons of unit vectors, the geometry that page develops on the sphere, anisotropy included.
A dual encoder scores by an inner product of two embeddings, so it shares GloVe's gauge freedom: the loss fixes the scores, not the geometry of either tower.
Eckart–Young gives the flat-weight theorem: with every co-occurrence observed and uniform weights, GloVe's optimum is the truncated SVD of the double-centered PMI matrix.
Each observed cell of the Poisson log-bilinear likelihood contributes the Bregman divergence of the exponential, whose quadratic with a tempered weight is GloVe's loss.
Centering rows and columns before a truncated SVD is two-sided PCA, which is what GloVe computes when every pair is observed and the weights are flat.
The nuclear norm's variational form, the least half sum of squared factor norms, is why weight decay pins GloVe's factorization at the balanced one.
GloVe trains by AdaGrad, the per-coordinate adaptive step behind RMSProp and Adam; the page shows its trained factorization is whatever that path leaves.
Word analogies are the classic probe of learned representations; the page shows exact parallelograms are facts about count ratios while nearest-neighbor answers depend on the basis.
Its Remark 2 reads a complex eigenvalue a + bi of a real matrix as a rotation and scaling of a real plane; Lemma 1 here is the unit-modulus case, which RotatE applies coordinate by coordinate.

Its Example 5 and Remark 3 turn the eigenvalues plus or minus i omega of a rotation generator into cosine and sine terms, the same correspondence between multiplying by e to the i theta and rotating the plane that Lemma 1 proves.
Its Proposition 2 says mined negatives carry false negatives; here every hidden true fact is a training negative, and the model that can represent antisymmetry learns it from them.
Its Proposition 1 bounds the rank of a learned bilinear scorer; DistMult and ComplEx are bilinear scorers of the same kind, one diagonal matrix per relation.
Its Theorem 1 shows a full-rank sign pattern of sign-rank three; ComplEx's expressiveness results (Trouillon et al. 2017) bound its dimension by exactly this sign-rank.
Its entity graph has untyped, weighted edges; a knowledge-graph embedding works with typed, directed edges and gives each type its own map.

Its Definition 4 is the CP decomposition. DistMult is a CP model of the knowledge base's 0/1 tensor whose head and tail factor matrices are one matrix, and that tie is what makes it symmetric (Proposition 3).

Temperature scaling is a one-parameter exponential family with natural parameter 1/τ and sufficient statistic the observed logit: its Theorem 7.1 gives Proposition 2's derivatives as a mean and a variance, and its Theorem 7.4 is the moment equation the optimum solves.

Theorem 3 is a statement about the score equation of its Theorem 1 along one direction of parameter space, and the temperature fit is its Theorem 6's Newton–Raphson iteration on a convex one-dimensional likelihood.

It calibrates retrieval scores with the reliability diagram and ECE and proves that a monotone recalibration preserves every ranking (its Theorem 2); Proposition 2(c) shows temperature scaling is not monotone in the confidence, so the order of confidences across contexts can change.

A calibrated confidence is the input to a decision to answer or abstain; Chow's rule, the risk–coverage curve, and conformal control of the wrong-answer rate are developed there, and this page stops at measuring and repairing the confidence.

Its calibration section supplies the binary apparatus this page generalizes: Dawid's definition, the reliability diagram and ECE, strict properness of the Brier score and log loss (its Theorem 2), and Murphy's binned Brier decomposition (its Theorem 3), which Theorem 1 extends to whole next-token distributions and to the log loss.
Theorem 1 is written in KL divergences: the refinement gap is KL(P ‖ C) and the reliability term KL(C ‖ F), and Gibbs's inequality (KL ≥ 0) is what makes each term a cost.

Proposition 3 shows that a nucleus covers the next token at its kept mass only if the model is calibrated; split conformal prediction (its Theorem 1) instead chooses the threshold on held-out data and guarantees marginal coverage with no calibration at all.
Its Theorem 6, Cramér's theorem for independent sample means, supplies the matching lower bound that makes Theorem 1's exponent log ρ exact rather than only an upper bound.

Theorem 2 is ridge regression's penalty moved off the origin: shrinking a logistic model toward the dictionary's subspace instead of toward zero, which is its Gaussian-prior reading with a nonzero prior mean.
Loughran and McDonald also weight dictionary words by tf–idf, the retrieval weighting that topic derives; this page cites that variant rather than re-deriving or testing it.
Its Theorem 3, the Chernoff bound, is the method of Theorem 1(a): exponentiate, apply Markov's inequality, and optimize the moment generating function, here for a three-valued token score.
Its Laplacian quadratic form, a sum of squared differences across edges, is the Dirichlet energy whose positivity with seed boundary values makes Theorem 3's harmonic solution unique.
Proposition 1's category world is multinomial naive Bayes on three collapsed categories (positive, negative, other); its development of the multinomial event model is the general case.
Its hitting-time machinery is the probabilistic side of Theorem 3(c): a word's induced polarity is twice the probability that a walk from it reaches a positive seed first, minus one.

Its Theorems 1 and 2 give binary logistic regression's score, Hessian, concavity, and IRLS; Theorem 1 here is the multiclass softmax version its Remark 27 defers, and Theorem 4 turns its Remark 8 on separation into theorems.

Both classifiers are maximum-likelihood fits, naive Bayes of the joint likelihood and logistic regression of the conditional one; Theorem 1's estimating equations are the score equations of the conditional likelihood.
Its Theorem 6, Dirichlet–multinomial conjugacy, is why add-α smoothing is a posterior mean, the smoothing whose effect on rare words Proposition 3(b) bounds.

Its correspondence between Gaussian priors and ridge penalties is what Proposition 3(a) specializes: weighting features by naive Bayes log-count ratios is a ridge penalty with a different prior variance for every word.
Its Theorem 1, the Robertson–Spärck Jones relevance weight, is the Bernoulli naive Bayes weight of Proposition 1(a) with relevance as the class.

Query likelihood scores a document with a smoothed multinomial, exactly naive Bayes's class-conditional model, and its Dirichlet smoothing (Theorem 1) is the background-smoothing alternative to add-α.

It develops the Gaussian, multinomial, and Bernoulli variants, Laplace smoothing as a conjugate update, calibration repair, and Ng and Jordan's comparison for Gaussian naive Bayes (its §7); this page proves the discrete-feature version of the generative bound, and what a multinomial vocabulary and Zipf's law do to it.

Its Theorem 6, the VC dimension of half-spaces, is what makes Ng and Jordan's discriminative sample complexity linear in the number of features, the side of their comparison this page cites rather than proves.
Theorem 1's convexity of the softmax log loss and the uniqueness arguments of Theorem 4 use its first- and second-order conditions for convexity.
Its §11 logistic lasso is the L1 counterpart of this page's ridge-penalized logistic regression on high-dimensional, sparse text features.
Its margin-based generalization bound (Theorem 6) is why the max-margin direction that Theorem 4 and gradient descent converge to is a good one to converge to.
Its convergence rates for convex smooth objectives govern Theorem 1's loss; on separable text the same gradient descent never converges in the weights, only in direction (Theorem 4).
The unsmoothed n-gram model is the maximum-likelihood estimate of each context's next-word multinomial, and its zero-frequency failure is what every smoother repairs.
The hierarchical Dirichlet language model shrinks each context toward the lower order and fits its prior strength by Type-II maximum likelihood, the parametric empirical Bayes of §28.7.
Good–Turing's adjusted count (r+1)N_{r+1}/N_r is Robbins' formula (§33.3, Theorem 2) with word types as policy holders, and inherits its instability where counts are sparse.
Relative frequencies maximize likelihood by Gibbs' inequality (the gap is the context count times a KL divergence), and smoothers are compared by held-out log-loss.
Kneser–Ney is read as an approximation to a hierarchical Pitman–Yor process — the two-parameter generalization of the Dirichlet process and its Chinese-restaurant representation.

Its Theorem 3, the second-order condition, makes the CRF objective on frozen encoder features strictly concave once the L2 penalty is added (Corollary 1), so every tagger on this page has one optimum.
Its Definition 3 is perfect calibration; Theorem 3 here is F1-optimal only for calibrated span marginals, and the held-out names show what miscalibration does to the threshold.

Backpropagation is the multivariate chain rule run in reverse; this page proves reverse accumulation on a general graph with fan-out and bounds products of recurrent Jacobians, both built on its chain rule.
Every training step follows the gradient of the cross-entropy, and the softmax's gradient p − y is the partial-derivative calculation this page builds its backpropagation on.
The smoothing-by-geometry theorem is the mean value theorem on a segment between two context embeddings, with the softmax's gradient bounded along it.
The softmax is the categorical exponential family: its Jacobian is the covariance of the one-hot vector, which makes the cross-entropy convex in the logits.
The output layer is a multinomial logit; its score identity, proved here for K classes, extends the canonical-link identity and forces moment matching at every stationary point.
Training a language model by cross-entropy is maximum likelihood, and its failure for a target never seen in training is why the unknown-word symbol needs word dropout.
The networks are trained by adaptive stochastic gradient descent; hidden-unit symmetry makes the objective non-convex, so the convex convergence rates proved there do not apply here.
Spectral norms bound the gradients through time, and Eckart–Young measures how much of Kneser–Ney's log-probability matrix lies beyond the softmax bottleneck's rank.
Dynamic evaluation is prequential coding: the network updates on each sentence after coding it, and the decoder replays the updates, so its bits per character are a code length.
Its Theorem 8, Hoeffding's inequality made uniform over a finite class by the union bound, is Theorem 4(c) here: how many samples make Monte Carlo minimum Bayes risk pick the exact decision.

Its Theorem 13, Jensen's inequality, and Example 7, the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality, bound BLEU's geometric mean of precisions by their arithmetic mean, the step Theorem 1 here uses to read the envelope.

It grades generated text against its source with a judge, the response to what this page proves overlap cannot see: a reversed fact moves an overlap score by one word's worth and a faithfulness judgment from true to false.
Its corrected prevalence estimators and agreement statistics treat a judge model as a noisy measurement, the alternative to reference overlap that Proposition 7's bias argument leaves standing.
Its paired tests and bootstrap intervals are the machinery this page withholds: the τ values and system gaps here are descriptive, and their uncertainty is the next topic's subject.
Held-out log-loss converges to the per-token cross-entropy because it is a ratio of two sample means over i.i.d. sentences, each governed by the strong law.
The standard error of held-out perplexity comes from the CLT and the delta method applied to the ratio estimator, with sentences rather than tokens as the independent units.
Minimizing empirical cross-entropy is maximizing likelihood, and the log score's strict propriety is why maximum likelihood rewards a model for reporting its true beliefs.
The AEP is proved here with Chebyshev's polynomial bound; Cramér's theorem sharpens the typical set's concentration to an exponential rate.
Held-out log-loss and AIC estimate the same quantity — expected out-of-sample cross-entropy — one by holding data out, the other by correcting the in-sample fit.

Kraft's inequality and the source-coding theorem are cited from there; this page adds McMillan's theorem, which extends Kraft to every uniquely decodable code, and makes the code exact with arithmetic coding.
Cross-entropy is entropy plus KL divergence (its Proposition 1); that decomposition makes the log score strictly proper and prices coding with the wrong model at KL bits per symbol.
An arithmetic code under a sequential model is a prequential code, and lzma's out-of-domain win on EDGAR text is adaptive (prequential) coding beating every static model.

Its orthogonality theorem holds for integer harmonics over a full period; the positional code's frequencies are geometric, not harmonic, so its Gram matrix is a stationary kernel rather than the identity.
A 2-D rotation is a linear map whose matrix composes by multiplication, so shifting a sinusoidal code is one block-diagonal rotation and RoPE scores pick up R(n − m).
The rotation by k steps is the matrix exponential exp(kA) of a block-skew generator, so k ↦ R(k) is a one-parameter group, the structure behind both the sinusoidal code and RoPE.
A complex-conjugate eigenvalue pair acts on its real plane as a rotation-scaling, which is exactly the block that commutes with a rotation and the block of an orthogonal matrix's normal form.
The sinusoidal kernel, normalized, is the characteristic function of the code's frequencies, and its large-dimension limit is a weak limit of characteristic functions.
That page models a passage buried in a long context as softly erased; ALiBi's horizon is one mechanism for such burial, a recency kernel under which far tokens weigh less than near ones.
A rotation applied to both query and key preserves their inner product; RoPE applies different rotations to the two, and what survives the inner product is exactly the rotation by their offset.

ALiBi's position factor is the Matérn-½ kernel, a product of positive-definite kernels stays positive definite, and a stationary kernel is a spectral measure, which is how this page reads the sinusoidal code.
ALiBi's attention is a Nadaraya–Watson smoother whose kernel is a product of a content kernel and an exponential kernel in time, so its bandwidth in position is the inverse slope.
On cyclic positions a stationary Gram matrix is circulant, diagonalized by the discrete Fourier basis exactly as the spectrum of an abelian Cayley graph is.

Its Remark 16 states Fisher's identity, the log-likelihood gradient as a posterior expectation of the complete-data gradient; Theorem 2 proves it for the noisy-OR bag likelihood and reads off the witness weights.
Its false negatives and unknown class prior in contrastive training are the retrieval cousin of Definition 5 here, where a pair the knowledge base forgot is labeled as unrelated.
Its entity graph is built from co-occurrence and embedding similarity; the facts this page extracts give such a graph typed, directed edges instead.
Its Proposition 2, Gibbs' inequality, is the whole proof of Theorem 1: the distant-supervision risk exceeds its minimum by an expected KL divergence from the expected distant label.
Theorem 2(b) is its Theorem 7.1 applied to the tempered family: the log-partition function's first and second derivatives in 1/τ are the mean and variance of log p, which give dH/dτ = Var(log p)/τ³.

Proposition 5's martingale has bounded increments on a finite vocabulary with a probability floor, so the Azuma–Hoeffding inequality (its Theorem 7) makes a sample's NLL concentrate around its path's entropy at an exponential rate.

The entropy of a next-token distribution is what temperature raises (Theorem 2), and the chain rule for entropy (its Theorem 1) is the identity behind Proposition 5: a sample's expected surprisal is its path's accumulated entropy.
Truncation's cost is a KL divergence: keeping mass m costs KL(p_S ‖ p) = −log m while the reverse direction is infinite, the asymmetry its section on forward and reverse KL develops.

The tempered distributions form an exponential family with natural parameter 1/τ and sufficient statistic log p, so annealing walks a curve in the dually flat geometry its Theorem 5 establishes for exponential families.

Ancestral sampling is sequential importance sampling with the model as its own proposal, and the identity E_q Π m(h_t) of Theorem 4(c) is an importance weight; tempering sequences are the standard bridge between distributions in SMC.
Theorem 2 is the integral test (its Theorem 8) with the remainder written out: a power-law tail bracketed between two integrals.
Theorems 1 and 3 evaluate Gamma-function integrals and ratios (its Definition 4 and Theorems 4–5), which set both exponents' constants.
Every exponent on this page that is not proved is an ordinary least-squares slope on log–log axes, or a vertex of a least-squares quadratic.
Chinchilla's Approach 3 is a Huber M-estimator of the five parameters of the loss law (its §15.11 and Theorem 11, Huber's minimax property).
Hoffmann and colleagues' exponent intervals are bootstrap percentiles and Besiroglu and colleagues' are bootstrap standard errors, the intervals the replication found too narrow.
Theorem 4's multiplier is the sensitivity theorem's shadow price (its Theorem 7, ∂p*/∂v = −ν*) for the compute budget 6ND = C: the loss one more FLOP buys.
Theorem 3 and Proposition 1 analyze gradient flow and one-pass SGD on a quadratic loss, whose convergence that topic proves (its Theorem 6 for SGD).
The sample-wise and model-wise risk curves of least squares, with the interpolation peak that the monotone power laws on this page leave out.
The Dirichlet process and its Chinese restaurant: its missing mass θ/(θ + n) and logarithmic type count are Theorem 1's case d = 0.

Its Definition 3 is the HMM, its Theorem 4 the factorization, and its Theorems 5, 7, and 8 the forward recursion, forward-backward smoothing, and Viterbi decoding, which Theorem 1 here generalizes from probabilities to arbitrary nonnegative potentials in either semiring.

Its Theorem 1 proves that the log-partition function's first two derivatives are the mean and variance of the sufficient statistic in one dimension; Theorem 2 here is the multivariate, conditional version that makes the CRF likelihood concave.
Its Theorem 6, Dirichlet-multinomial conjugacy, makes the HMM tagger's add-alpha counts the posterior mean under a Dirichlet prior on each row (Proposition 1).
Its Theorem 3, the second-order condition, turns Theorem 2's negative semidefinite Hessian into concavity of the CRF's conditional log-likelihood, and strict concavity once the L2 penalty is added.

Its Section 7 compares naive Bayes with logistic regression, the classic generative-discriminative pair; Theorem 3 here shows the HMM and the indicator-feature CRF are the same pair for sequences, with one family of conditionals and two estimators.
Its Corollary 1, Bonferroni's inequality, is the bound on the size of reporting whichever of k metrics rejects, the upper end of Proposition 5.
Its Theorem 3, Efron–Bickel–Freedman consistency for a scalar mean, is the one-dimensional case of the bootstrap step in Theorem 2 here, where corpus BLEU is a function of ten pooled means at once.

Its Theorem 7, the multivariate central limit theorem, starts the proof of Theorem 2; its Theorem 8, the scalar delta method, is extended there to corpus BLEU's ten statistics and fails at the brevity penalty's kink in Proposition 3.
Its Theorems 1, 3, and 5 prove the Bonferroni, Holm, and Benjamini–Hochberg guarantees that Proposition 5 and the finance case study apply to the 45 summarizer pairs and to metric shopping.

Its Theorem 3, that a p-value is uniform under a continuous null, is the equality case of Theorem 1 here, whose randomization p-values are only superuniform because swaps of identical outputs leave atoms.

Its Theorem 3, that a permutation test averaged over a finite group is exact under invariance, is the full-group case of Theorem 1 here; its Theorem 1, the sign test's null distribution, is what Proposition 1 reduces McNemar's test to.
Its Theorem 4, Hoeffding's inequality, bounds how far a Monte Carlo p-value from B random swaps can stray from the full-group p-value, which sets how many draws Theorem 1's test needs.
Its confidence sequences and e-values allow an evaluation to be checked as test data arrive, which every fixed-sample test on this page forbids.
Unigram LM piece probabilities are maximum-likelihood estimates over latent segmentations, and WordPiece merges by the gain in unigram log-likelihood.
Tokenizers are compared as codes: a piece costs its Shannon code length −log p, and the Viterbi segmentation is the shortest encoding under the Unigram LM's code.
The vocabulary size is read off a two-part code — bits to spell the vocabulary plus bits to code the corpus with it — whose total has an interior minimum.
EM's monotonicity for the Unigram LM rests on Jensen's inequality and on Gibbs' inequality (KL ≥ 0), which makes normalized expected counts the exact M-step.

Its Theorem 5 gives the Dirichlet moments behind the topic–topic matrix R = E[θθᵀ], and its Theorem 6 is the Dirichlet–multinomial conjugacy that Lemma 1 integrates and Proposition 6 reads as posterior means.

Its Theorem 2 says a Gibbs update is a Metropolis–Hastings step that always accepts, which gives Corollary 1's invariance; its Remark 10 names collapsed Gibbs for LDA, and Theorem 2 here derives the conditional it leaves implicit.

Its Theorem 1 proves that the log-partition function's derivative is the mean of the sufficient statistic in one dimension; Lemma 2 is the Dirichlet case, whose sufficient statistic is log θ, proved directly.
Its Theorem 1 reads Dirichlet smoothing as a posterior mean; Proposition 6's topic and proportion estimates are the same posterior mean, given one sample of the topic assignments.

Latent semantic analysis projects documents onto a low-rank subspace in Euclidean norm, with coordinates of both signs; LDA projects them in KL divergence onto a polytope inside the word simplex (the remark after Proposition 2).
Its Theorem 2 is the CAVI coordinate update and its Proposition 1 the conjugate case, the expected natural parameter; Theorem 3 here applies both to LDA's three blocks of factors.
Its Proposition 2, Gibbs' inequality, makes Proposition 2 here a projection: fitting a document's topic proportions minimizes the KL divergence from its word frequencies to the topic polytope.

Its Definition 1 and Proposition 2 are the Dirichlet distribution and its conjugacy; its Chinese restaurant process is the K-free relative of the Pitman–Yor restaurants that seat the finance corpus's content nouns.
The multivariate chain rule multiplies Jacobians; for a residual block the Jacobian is the identity plus the branch's, and multiplying those out over layers is the identity path of Theorem 2.
A residual block x + f(x) is one step of Euler's method for the flow x' = f(x), so a deep stack of small updates discretizes a continuous trajectory of the tokens.
Ordinary least squares is an orthogonal projection; LayerNorm's centering is the projection off the intercept column, the first half of its geometry in Proposition 3.
A Gaussian vector's norm concentrates in a thin shell at radius √d, so LayerNorm barely moves one at large d and acts only when the stream's norm drifts, as it does with depth in a pre-LN stack.
Many nearly orthogonal directions fit in few dimensions, which is why a 32-dimensional stream can carry 256 random token embeddings that an induction head still copies correctly.
Its convergence theorem says a mixing chain forgets where it started; Theorem 1 here is the contraction step behind that, in the Dobrushin form, and attention plus the skip is a scaled lazy walk.
A head's OV circuit W_V W_O has rank at most the head width, and the composition scores are ratios of Frobenius norms, both read through the singular value decomposition.
The descent lemma ties a safe step size to the curvature; post-LN's large gradients near the output at initialization are why such blocks need learning-rate warmup and pre-LN ones do not.
The residual stream is a shared space that each head reads and writes through low-rank projections, so two heads communicate only through the subspaces where one writes and the other reads.
Gradient descent is the Euler discretization of gradient flow, the ODE along which the page proves that the word and context Gram matrices' difference is conserved.
The second derivative of the cell loss at its optimum is the local weight that skip-gram puts on each word–context pair, which makes it a weighted least squares near the optimum.
Each cell of the negative-sampling objective is a logistic regression likelihood with a canonical link, strictly concave in the score, which is why its optimum is unique.
InfoNCE is the softmax counterpart of negative sampling: its optimal critic is PMI up to a per-query constant, while skip-gram's binary loss pins the logit to PMI minus log k.
Both pages draw negatives from a noise distribution; there the question is which negatives to mine for retrieval, here what the unigram-to-the-0.75 noise makes the optimum factorize.
A dual encoder's score is an inner product of two embeddings, the same factorized form as word and context vectors, with the same rank ceiling and the same gauge freedom.

Negative sampling is a classifier between observed pairs and noise pairs, so its optimal logit is the log density ratio plus the log prior odds of that page's classification identity, here PMI minus log k.
The cross-entropy decomposition turns the negative-sampling loss into a count-weighted sum of Bernoulli KL divergences, which is what skip-gram minimizes at low rank.
Each cell's KL term is a Bregman divergence of the Bernoulli log-partition, so skip-gram with negative sampling is an exponential-family (logistic) PCA in natural parameters.
Truncated SVD of shifted PPMI is the uniform-weight, Eckart–Young counterpart that the page compares with skip-gram's count-weighted factorization of the same matrix.
Word2vec is stochastic gradient descent on a factorized loss; the page shows that its gradient flow conserves the difference of the word and context Gram matrices, which fixes the factorization.
Word2vec's embeddings are an early learned representation; the page shows that its objective fixes only the product of word and context vectors, so similarity depends on the optimizer.
DeepWalk applies skip-gram to random-walk co-occurrences, so the implicit-factorization result proved here is the one behind its matrix-factorization reading.

The Zipf and discrete power laws are distributions on the positive integers; we use their probability mass functions, tails, and normalizers throughout.

The Zipfian head is the stopword list and the long tail is where IDF weights are largest; TF-IDF inherits this topic's distribution.
Zipf's law is derived as the maximum-entropy distribution at fixed mean log-rank, with optimality from Gibbs' inequality (KL divergence is nonnegative).
